He believes covered calls will be an increasingly attractive strategy for Australian investors seeking risk-adjusted income, particularly as the traditional dividend yield is near multi-decade lows. He sees this as part of a broader diversification within the income investing landscape.
quote: We've seen a lot of interest within covered calls. So our old ETF has outperformed the broader market by around about 4 or 5% so far this year. And you're getting income from different sources like from the options market. And when you're talking about risk adjusted income, I have a feeling that cupboard calls are going to be one that Australian investors gravitate towards.
episode_title: Investors turn to ETFs amid CGT changes

headline: AI and semiconductor thematic ETFs dominating flows, up ~80% YTD, led by SK Hynix, Nvidia and Samsung
reasoning: Jocum notes that thematic ETFs are capturing 5-10% of total ETF flows over three successive months of over $5 billion in inflows. The biggest driver is the AI trade, particularly semiconductors, which are up almost 80% year to date. Key performers include SK Hynix, Nvidia and Samsung. He also highlights investor interest in second-order AI beneficiaries via Global X's AI Infrastructure ETF (AINF), which has seen record monthly flows and is outperforming the broader market by up to 20% YTD.
quote: We're seeing most of the flows going is into the AI trade. So we've seen a lot of interest in semiconductors given the huge ramp up in performance, up almost 80% so far this year, led by the likes of SK Hynix, Nvidia and Samsung. But Andrew, what's really interesting is we've seen investors also gravitate towards the second order beneficiaries of this AI trade. So the global Artificial Intelligence Infrastructure ETF, AI and F has actually seen has seen flows every single month since we've launched it last year. Last month was a record month for it. And we're starting to see these AI ETFs really outperform the broader market by up to 20% so far this year.

headline: Global X's Marc Jocum flags a major re-rating in cybersecurity stocks after a deep drawdown, with the BUG ETF recovering to become Australia's best-performing ETF last month.
reasoning: The Global X Cybersecurity ETF (BUG) suffered a 40% drawdown after being caught up in the broader SaaS sell-off, but rebounded sharply to become the best-performing ETF on the Australian market last month. Jocum attributes this re-rating to growing recognition that cybersecurity names can defend against AI-driven hacking threats and malicious software. He notes cybersecurity software names still trade at a significant discount to semiconductor names, and sees the tide potentially turning. He highlights Anthropic's model-use restrictions as further evidence of mounting cyber risk that benefits the sector.
quote: I think that cybersecurity stocks in particular, and our cybersecurity ETF bug was actually one of the worst performing so far this year because it got, um, tied into this whole SaaS apocalypse trade where software names were sold off heavily. It was in a 40% drawdown. But funnily enough, last month the bug ETF was the best performing ETF on the Australian market. We saw a huge rerating in cybersecurity stocks. As we're starting to see to your point that the threat of hacking, of cybersecurity, of cryptography, all these imminent threats can be solved by these cybersecurity names. So I think that there was a huge rerating about the potential that cybersecurity names can actually offer as a defensible source of protecting against AI hackers and against malicious software. And we've even seen now with anthropic in the US that there's been restrictions around the the use case for some of the models that are being used. So for me, I think cybersecurity names were very unloved. There's still a huge discount of software names to semiconductor names. Whether that rebounds is another question, but perhaps the tide has turned for cybersecurity names.

headline: 91% of Australian ETF flows remain in passive index products despite active ETF proliferation
reasoning: Jocum notes that while active ETFs now represent over half of new ETF launches in Australia and generate about 40% of revenue, they only account for 20% of assets under management. More strikingly, 91% of actual fund flows are going into passive index-based ETFs, reflecting strong and consistent demand from Australian investors for low-cost, transparent, straightforward products. He contrasts this with overseas trends where active ETFs are growing rapidly.
quote: Even though over half of the new ETFs coming out in the Australian market are active ETFs, and about 40% of the revenue is from active ETFs. About 20% of the market is currently active, meaning 80% of the assets are in index based ETFs. But the the eye watering stat, Andrew, is that 91% of the flows are going into index based ETFs. So you're seeing consistent demand for low cost ETFs that are transparent that say what the name does on the tin.

headline: Global X's Marc Jocum sees index-based ETFs continuing to dominate Australian flows, driven by low cost, transparency, and CGT sensitivity around active manager turnover.
reasoning: 91% of ETF flows in Australia are going into index-based ETFs despite active ETFs making up over half of new issuance and 40% of revenue. Jocum argues that once fees are included, active ETFs struggle to compete, and he believes upcoming capital gains tax changes will make investors even more conscious of portfolio turnover and concentration risk inherent in active strategies. He expects index ETF investing to continue growing and sees little sign of that trend slowing.
quote: the eye watering stat, Andrew, is that 91% of the flows are going into index based ETFs. So you're seeing consistent demand for low cost ETFs that are transparent that say what the name does on the tin. There's no issues around disclosures. So I think that index ETFs are going to be a formidable force. There are a lot of active ETFs coming to market. But the harsh evidence suggests that once you include fees, and I have a feeling these capital gains taxes are going to really make investors conscious around turnover, around the actual concentration risks as some of these active managers are placing. I really think that index ETF investing is going to continue to go up into the right here in Australia, and I see little sign of that slowing down.
episode_title: Investors turn to ETFs amid CGT changes

headline: Record $2.4bn inflows into Australian equity ETFs driven by CGT budget changes and shift toward income investing
reasoning: Marc Jocum notes that Australian equity ETFs saw a record $2.4 billion in inflows last month, representing almost half of total ETF flows — the highest since August 2023. He attributes this partly to pre-existing trends but also to a new catalyst from the federal budget's capital gains tax proposals, which are prompting investors to think more locally. A notable rotation into income-based investing is underway, with around $250 million flowing into index-based high dividend yield ETFs. Investors are seeking after-tax income options, and ETFs are providing that access.
quote: Around about $2.4 billion came in last, last month, which represents around about almost half of the total flows going into ETFs, which is the highest we've seen since about 2023 and August 2023. But what's really interesting, Andrew, to a point, is we're seeing this rotation into income based investing. And I think this has been a bit of a shift for Australian investors, where we saw around about a quarter of $1 billion come into index based high dividend yield ETFs. So I do think this has been a catalyst. And it now seems that investors are trying to look for after tax income options.
episode_title: Investors turn to ETFs amid CGT changes
